headline: The growth hormone research
body: And almost everyone quoting it only shows you one half.
punch: Both halves are real studies. That's what makes this interesting.

headline: Two camps
body: One says GH reliably adds height in short children. The other says it does nothing, or makes things worse. Neither side is making its evidence up.
punch: The disagreement is inside the literature — not between honest and dishonest people.

headline: Side one
body: Meta-analyses of children with idiopathic short stature: treated groups ended 0.84 standard deviations taller than controls. Roughly four to six centimetres of adult height.
punch: That's the number the field usually quotes.

headline: Side two
body: A 1997 study of boys short but not GH-deficient: untreated reached 162.0 cm on average. GH-treated reached 154.2 cm. The treated boys ended up shorter.
punch: Nearly eight centimetres — in the wrong direction.

headline: So how are both true
body: Different populations and different designs. Pooled analyses lean on idiopathic short stature cohorts, many uncontrolled. The unfavourable results come from controlled comparisons in non-deficient boys through puberty.
punch: Who was studied changes the answer completely.

headline: Which is the actual lesson
body: Not that GH works. Not that it doesn't. That the effect depends on who you are, and nobody quoting a single number to you has told you which population it came from.
punch: Ask which cohort the number came from. Every time.

headline: And the cost
body: Where gains do occur they run to roughly thirty-five thousand dollars per inch of adult height.
punch: Years of daily injections for less than one shoe size.

headline: For people of normal height
subhead: THERE IS NO DATA AT ALL
body: No trial has tested GH for height in normal-statured people, because nobody would run it. Both camps above studied short children.
punch: If a number exists for that population somebody invented it.

headline: What I got wrong
body: First I said GH can't work if you're not deficient. Then I over-corrected and said the meta-analyses settled it. Both were too clean — the literature is genuinely split.
punch: Getting it right matters more than sounding certain.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
